summary:
Azerbaijan offers no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Same-sex couples have no standing: marriage and civil unions are neither performed nor recognised, and same-sex couples may not adopt children. Trans people cannot change the gender marker on official documents, although a name change to match gender identity is available. ILGA-Europe has ranked Azerbaijan last, 49th of 49, in its annual European comparison every year since 2015, attributing the position to a near-total absence of legal protection.

Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017, national police in the capital detained at least 100 members of the LGBTIQ community in raids conducted ostensibly against prostitution; at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the arrests formed part of a wave of detentions ahead of an international sporting event. Detainees were subjected to beatings, interrogation, forced medical examinations and blackmail, and a foreign government's 2017 human rights report recorded police threats of rape and the use of electric shocks. Azerbaijan acknowledged the case in 2019, and in April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the arrests and mistreatment.

In July 2023, officers raided a private birthday party at which queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed. In March 2024 a trans woman was murdered in the capital and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate; nothing in the record indicates that the authorities treat the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring serious inquiry.

Hostility is carried by official and semi-official media. After a Women's Day march in 2024 demanding access to trans healthcare, the state-affiliated Real TV channel aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people. Media monitoring of 428 pieces in 2023 found 77% hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and politicians and officials have used discriminatory language to shape public perception. In one incident an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag in a Baku cafe.

Discrimination has direct economic consequences. Trans people are rejected from jobs and housing and pushed into black-market work and precarious accommodation; one profiled woman, aged 29, was arrested, denied housing and employment, and left dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer closed. A family forcibly transported an 18-year-old woman to the capital after she came out.

Conscription is a further exposure point. Azerbaijan mandates military service for able-bodied men aged 18 to 35, under which LGBTQIA+ enlistees can be declared unfit for service under Articles 18/b (personality disorders) and 17/b (reactive psychoses and neurotic disorders) of the Regulation on Military Medical Examinations, and queer conscripts often conceal their orientation to avoid hazing.

The record also shows that state institutions have been held to account in a school case. In April 2019 a 14-year-old girl in the capital attempted suicide after homophobic bullying at her school; the principal took no action, attributed the attempt to family difficulties and did not call an ambulance, and she died in hospital two days later. The school director, deputy director and psychologist were dismissed, and on 24 October 2019 the Sabail District Court of Baku sentenced the principal to 2 years and 2.5 months of restricted liberty plus 18,500 AZN in compensation. A Ministry of Education anti-bullying action plan with a new hotline followed on 13 May 2019.
tangentialFactors:
Azerbaijan's constitution guarantees freedom of expression, and the Azerbaijan Press Council, founded in 2003, handles complaints under a Press Code of Conduct; it is not known whether it has assessed complaints that state-controlled media used homosexuality to discredit government critics. A foreign government's 2017 report recorded interference with expression, assembly and association through intimidation, incarceration on questionable charges and blocking of websites.

The age of consent is 16 for both heterosexual and homosexual sex. By law no groups are excluded from blood donation apart from people infected with HIV/AIDS, though it is unknown whether men who have sex with men are de facto permitted to donate.

Controversy over hosting international events has flared repeatedly, notably around the 2012 international song contest and the 2017 sporting event that preceded the police raids; critics have argued that Azerbaijan should not be permitted to host such events while it discriminates against LGBTQIA+ people.

LGBTQIA+ media does exist despite the climate: gay.az, the first news website for LGBTQIA+ people, launched 25 May 2011, and Minority Magazine, founded in December 2015 and registered as an NGO in August 2017. A documentary about a trans man premiered in the capital on 25 November 2017 with embassy support, drawing about 80 people. The 2017 crackdown and the 2023 party raid are the same pattern of police action seen a decade apart, and both involved forced medical examination as an instrument of control.
localsOnly:
Community infrastructure is established but small. The Gender Resource Center, founded in 2020, operates as a queer-feminist platform in response to the lack of safe space and resources for people of different genders and sexual orientations. Gender and Development, created in 2007, runs local projects in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, and its shadow report to the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women at the 44th session documents state-approved ignorance, employment discrimination, hostile official and private media, forced marriages, and the impossibility of changing identity documents for trans women; the organisation serves more than 200 LBT people.

AZAD LGBT ran in-person programming in the capital, including film nights attended by a local psychologist who joined post-screening discussions, and launched a website in 2015 providing free online education tools. Nafas LGBTI Azerbaijan Alliance regularly holds talks with the EU Delegation and other European embassies about the difficulties LGBTQ people face. Minority Azerbaijan's Vahid Aliyev has criticised media unprofessionalism on these questions.

Trans residents may change their name to match their gender identity even though the gender marker itself is fixed. Men aged 18 to 35 remain subject to conscription, and the medical-unfitness articles give a formal route out of service that nonetheless requires disclosure to military medical examiners.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or border-screening rules for trans visitors, including whether passport gender markers are checked on arrival or whether entry can be refused on those grounds. That question is unresolved here and should not be read as carrying any particular answer.

The inventory does not establish whether Azerbaijan has hate-crime legislation covering offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity, nor whether any such offences have been prosecuted. The enforcement status of the April 2024 European Court of Human Rights ruling, including any payment of just satisfaction or legislative follow-up, is not sourced.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare for a short-term visitor, the availability of hormone prescriptions, and the practical operation of the document-change prohibition are not documented beyond the CEDAW shadow report's statement that changing identity documents is impossible for trans women. Whether men who have sex with men can in fact donate blood is likewise unknown, as is whether the Press Council has ever handled a complaint about state media content.
